def: The standard fertilizer measure: pounds of actual nitrogen spread over 1,000 sq ft. Tall fescue needs about 3–4 a year. The fertilizer calculator converts it to pounds of product.
The three numbers on a bag: % nitrogen, % phosphate and % potash. A 50 lb bag of 28-0-12 contains 14 lb of nitrogen.
Modern lawn cultivars of tall fescue: finer, denser and darker than the old pasture type (KY-31).
A 1943 forage (pasture) variety of tall fescue. It's tough but coarse, clumpy and pale in lawns, and MU restricts it to roadsides.
Tall fescue marketed as spreading by rhizomes. K-State found its rhizomes tiny (about 3 mm), so it doesn't fill bare spots the way bluegrass does.
A cool-season grass that spreads by rhizomes to fill gaps. It's less drought-resilient than tall fescue, so use about 10% in a rain-fed KC mix.
Grasses that grow most in spring and fall and slow down in summer heat: tall fescue, Kentucky bluegrass, ryegrass.
Bermudagrass and zoysia: green in summer, tan from the first frost until May. In a fescue lawn they're weeds.
The band across the middle of the U.S., including Kansas City, where neither cool- nor warm-season grasses are perfectly adapted. Tall fescue is the best compromise.
A lawn's drought survival mode: leaves turn brown but the crowns stay alive, and it greens up after soaking rain.
The growing point at the base of a grass plant. As long as the crowns live, the lawn recovers.
An herbicide that stops seeds from sprouting (e.g., crabgrass preventer). It stops grass seed too.
An herbicide that kills weeds that are already growing.
Selective products kill certain plants (e.g., broadleaf weeds) without harming lawn grass. Non-selective ones (glyphosate) kill anything green they touch.
An additive that helps spray stick to and soak into leaves. Some labels require it (Tenacity used post-emergent); some forbid it (Tenacity at seeding).
How long a herbicide label says to wait before seeding a treated area: weeks for some products, 4–6 months for prodiamine.
Weeds with wide leaves and net-like veins (dandelion, clover, henbit), as opposed to grassy weeds such as crabgrass.
A weed that sprouts in fall, flowers in spring and dies by early summer (henbit, chickweed), so fall is the time to control it.
Pulling finger-sized plugs of soil to relieve compaction and open the soil for seed, water and air. Best done right before overseeding in September.
Spreading seed into an existing lawn to thicken it (4–5 lb of tall fescue per 1,000 sq ft).
Seeding in late fall or winter when it's too cold to sprout; the seed waits in the soil for spring. A fallback if you miss fall seeding.
The share of a bag that's live seed of the kind you paid for: purity × germination. A tag showing 98% purity and 85% germination is 83% PLS.
Seed certified by a state agency as true to its variety name.
The National Turfgrass Evaluation Program: independent, multi-year cultivar trials at university sites across the U.S., including Manhattan, KS and Columbia, MO.
The Turfgrass Water Conservation Alliance, which qualifies cultivars that keep their green cover under drought stress in multi-site trials.
Water lost from soil and leaves. ET₀ is the reference value weather models calculate; a lawn uses a fraction of it (this site uses 0.8).
The trigger for many tasks: crabgrass sprouts at ~55°F, tomatoes want 60°F+, peppers and melons 65°F+, and garlic and bulbs go in below 60°F.
The soil pH MU reports, measured in a salt solution. It typically reads about half a unit lower than a water-pH test.
A running total of warmth used to predict weed and insect timing. For crabgrass, plant bloom cues such as redbud are often more reliable.
The median date of the last spring or first fall 32°F freeze. At KCI they're April 13 and October 24, and 1 year in 10 the spring freeze comes after April 29.
Gradually moving indoor seedlings into sun and wind over 7–10 days before transplanting.
Scattering fertilizer beside growing plants in midseason, for example tomatoes at first fruit set.
Sowing small batches every few weeks for a steady harvest instead of one glut.
A plant that pests prefer, such as Blue Hubbard squash, grown to lure them away from the main crop.
Determinate tomatoes stop at a set size and ripen in a flush (good for canning). Indeterminate types keep growing and producing until frost (need tall cages).
A named, cultivated variety, such as 'Titan GLX' tall fescue or 'Celebrity' tomato.
Kansas City's plant hardiness zone: an average coldest winter night of −5 to 0°F.
A spongy layer of undecomposed stems between the soil and the grass. Tall fescue rarely builds much, and clippings don't cause it.
The main summer fungal disease of tall fescue in KC, driven by warm, humid nights and extra nitrogen.
An invasive beetle that kills ash trees; confirmed in the KC area since 2012.
When lettuce, spinach or cilantro flowers in heat or long days and turns bitter.
The first blush of color on a tomato. Picked then and ripened indoors, it tastes just as good and avoids cracking and squirrels.
